reasons: The excerpt explicitly advises replacing generic praise with proof that reinforces the particular claim and objection, including testimonial videos with before-and-afters and reviews filtered for that claim.
The completion condition is supported by the source's described stronger layout: a direct before-and-after testimonial matching the promoted claim.
This accurately presents the source's stated principle that a smaller amount of highly relevant proof works better than a larger amount of irrelevant generic proof.
It does not invent a numerical minimum or a relevance metric.

The source expressly characterizes trust badges and footer security seals as low-quality and ineffective, while describing guarantees and returns policies as generic table stakes rather than needle-moving trust signals.
The candidate preserves the distinction that a returns policy can matter while not being a differentiating trust signal.

The candidate faithfully summarizes the source's illustrative contrast between no reviews, a generic testimonial, and badges versus photo reviews plus a direct before-and-after testimonial that proves the promoted angle.
It appropriately retains uncertainty about validating a skin-firmness percentage statistic.

The source supports presenting a money-back risk reversal after proof in the pictured layout and calls it table stakes, but it does not establish that this action depends specifically on candidate 52366's claim-relevance-proof action.
Remove or qualify the stated depends_on relation; the excerpt presents the risk reversal as an additional layout element rather than a formal prerequisite contingent on that candidate.

The source offers four testimonials across slightly different demographics as an illustrative aspiration: “if we had like four ... that would be amazing,” not as an idealized target or prescribed count.
Revise the action to present approximately four as a nonbinding example of adding more demographic variety, rather than “ideally four.”
The supplied excerpt names the site as “bayard.com,” whereas the candidate identifies it as “Baymard.com.” The excerpt alone cannot support that spelling correction or current URL.
Retain the recommendation to consult the named ecommerce UX research source, but use the source's literal site name or explicitly flag the name as uncertain.
The sub-10%-of-AOV recommendation, its scope across shipping, tax, fees, and other added checkout expenses, and the qualification that it may vary by brand are supported.

The asserted depends_on relation to consulting the external research source is not supported. The excerpt presents the threshold as the speaker's internal finding and does not make research consultation a prerequisite for applying it.

The source expressly recommends considering removal of delivery-time estimates when actual delivery is slow, while warning that ambiguity lowers conversion and requiring a split test to determine whether the tradeoff offsets abandonment.
The 7-to-10-day testing period is correctly qualified as dependent on revenue, and the candidate notes that material impact is undefined.
The source presents faster delivery and fast-delivery options as alternatives, so the alternative relation is supported.

The source supports both alternatives: improve actual delivery speed where possible, or offer fast delivery options at checkout, and it notes that regional shipping constraints may prevent the first option.

The completion condition only recognizes the fast-delivery-options branch. It incorrectly leaves an actual faster-delivery implementation incomplete unless checkout options are also added. Completion should allow either stated alternative.
The source supports treating card-detail distrust as a trust issue, especially for newer brands, and recommends avoiding a scam-like appearance and reinforcing good proof.
The source also explicitly calls for more social proof and brand presence, but the stated action omits those components despite the title and claim including them.

The depends_on relation to the specific landing-page claim-proof candidate is not established. The source calls for good proof generally, not proof contingent on that particular landing-page implementation.
The excerpt directly says not to force account creation and, if the Shopify setting is enabled, to turn it off so people need not create accounts.
The candidate preserves the source's uncertainty about whether this is actually Shopify's default rather than presenting the platform behavior as verified fact.
The action accurately includes all listed measures: remove as many fields as possible, make as many optional as possible, and enable Shop Pay, Apple Pay, and other fast checkout options.
The source itself makes the “instantaneous” characterization, so the completion wording does not add an unsupported performance threshold.
The source expressly warns not to rush into free returns or an overly consumer-favorable policy, particularly in fashion, because it can increase returns and harm profit and operations.
The candidate retains the source's unresolved tradeoff: a more generous policy can be tested but may need to be withdrawn if it harms profitability.
The candidate correctly treats the ending as unresolved rather than inferring a completed recommendation from the cut-off sentence.
It also preserves the source's stated ambiguity over whether the cited abandonment reason concerns newly added charges or a price that changes between the landing page and cart/checkout.
The source explicitly says that 43% of abandoners were only browsing and that abandonment therefore cannot be reduced to zero.
The candidate accurately distinguishes those shoppers from the remaining abandonment reasons the source says can be addressed.

omissions.description: The source specifically recommends ordering photo reviews first; candidates mention photo reviews but do not represent this ordering recommendation.
omissions.quote: On the right, we've got reviews with photos sorted first.

source_limitations: The excerpt begins mid-thought, so preceding context for the opening statement is unavailable.
The excerpt cuts off mid-sentence while discussing upfront total-cost transparency, preventing confirmation of the intended recommendation.
Several abandonment percentages and checkout assertions are attributed to an external research site, but the excerpt does not provide its methodology, scope, date, or underlying study details.
The cited research website is transcribed as “bayard.com”; the excerpt alone cannot verify its spelling, current URL, or the claims attributed to it.
The sub-10% additional-cost threshold is explicitly described as an internal finding and as potentially brand-specific, not as a universally validated rule.
